surveyDefinition.title: Bottled Water — consumer survey (Global)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each respondent belongs to, based on consumption occasions, purchase behaviour, product requirements and satisfaction drivers.

segments.name: Convenience-Led Buyers
segments.description: Buy single-serve bottles for immediate consumption while commuting, traveling, or out of the home. Prioritize availability and portability over price. Often purchase from convenience stores, vending machines, or food service.

segments.name: Bulk-Purchase Households
segments.description: Buy large multi-packs or gallon jugs for home consumption by multiple household members. Price-sensitive, driven by value for money and consistent quality. Typically shop at supermarkets or warehouse clubs.

segments.name: Premium Quality Buyers
segments.description: Choose premium or enhanced waters (e.g., mineral, alkaline, functional) for taste, health benefits, or lifestyle. Low price sensitivity, high interest in provenance and quality cues. Often buy single-serve premium bottles.

segments.name: Eco-Conscious Customers
segments.description: Concerned about plastic waste and environmental impact. May buy bottled water out of necessity but actively seek recycled packaging, larger formats, or alternative brands. Open to switching to filtered or tap water if quality is assured.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Bottled Water buyers worldwide. It asks how people use Bottled Water, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories. This global view is not a separate fieldwork exercise: it selects the strongest questions from the regional surveys and blends their percentages using population-style regional weights.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults worldwide who buy or use Bottled Water for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Individuals who buy bottled water for their own consumption; Households that regularly purchase bottled water for home use. Excluded: Businesses purchasing bottled water for office supply or resale; Institutional buyers (e.g., hospitals, schools) purchasing for patients or staff.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Everyday consumers buy bottled water for personal consumption, pay for it themselves at retail, and decide which brand to purchase at the point of sale. While businesses may purchase bottled water for offices, the dominant and defining buyer is the individual consumer.
respondentBehaviours: Purchases bottled water at least weekly
Chooses between still, sparkling, flavored, and functional waters
Influenced by convenience, taste, brand trust, and health perceptions
May buy in bulk (multi-packs) or single-serve on-the-go
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Consumption Behaviour & Occasion Context
sections.covers: Establishes how respondents use bottled water, in what situations, and with what frequency, to segment by usage context.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Channel Behaviour
sections.covers: Covers what triggers a purchase, where they buy, how often they restock, and what they typically spend.

sections.label: Product, Packaging & Value Requirements
sections.covers: Explores must-have product attributes, packaging preferences, sustainability claims, and price-value trade-offs.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Switching Risk
sections.covers: Measures overall satisfaction, identifies friction points, and assesses likelihood to switch or reduce bottled water use.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: The survey opens by establishing who drinks bottled water and in what situations, then moves through the purchase journey from trigger to channel to spend, then explores product and packaging preferences including sustainability, and closes with satisfaction and switching risk. This arc separates the four segments by their consumption context, purchase patterns, and product priorities.

questions.question: How often do you personally drink bottled water?
questions.insight: Top response: About once a day (28.00%).
questions.distributionNote: Convenience-Led Buyers and Bulk-Purchase Households drive frequent daily consumption, while occasional usage is spread across all segments.

questions.question: Who are you usually buying bottled water for?

segmentModel.tie_break: Question bb5 (What size bottle of water do you usually buy?) is the most direct behavioural self-report to settle ties: single-serve signals convenience, multi-pack/gallon signals bulk household, and premium sizes are less relevant, while eco-conscious often choose larger formats to reduce plastic.
notes: Scoring focuses on explicit behavioural choices (location, trigger, size, type, packaging concern) rather than generic frequency or satisfaction.
Eco-conscious segment is identified primarily through stated concern about plastic waste and preference for eco-friendly packaging, plus intention to reduce consumption.
Premium segment is identified through choice of enhanced/mineral/alkaline waters, willingness to pay more, and quality cues.
Convenience segment is identified through out-of-home consumption, single-serve purchases, and purchase triggers of thirst while out.
Family bulk buyers are identified through buying for household, stocking up, and large formats.
14 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.
